summary.text: For exponents \(2,3,4\), congruences for a number and its reversal in terms of their digit sum and weighted digit sums force the digit sum to be divisible by \(3^n\); the digit bound then shows that any admissible number no larger than \(10^{3^{n-2}}-1\) must have exactly \(3^{n-2}\) digits, all equal to 9, while the all-nines number itself is divisible by \(3^n\). For \(n\ge5\), repeating the 27-digit palindromic block \(100000001979999979100000001\) exactly \(3^{n-5}\) times gives a smaller palindrome divisible by \(3^n\): the block supplies a factor \(3^5\), and its geometric repetition factor supplies \(3^{n-5}\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(R(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(m\). Thus, if
\[
m=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i10^i,
\qquad 0\le d_i\le 9,
\]
where \(d_{\ell-1}\ne0\), then
\[
R(m)=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i10^{\ell-1-i}.
\]
This definition also handles a zero at the units place in the usual way: after reversal it becomes an initial zero and hence does not affect the resulting integer.

For a positive integer \(N\), \(a(N)\) is the least positive multiple \(m=kN\), with \(k>0\), for which \(N\mid R(m)\), provided such an integer exists. In all cases considered below we explicitly produce such an integer, so the alternative value \(0\) in the definition of the sequence never enters.

We prove that for every \(n\ge2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

We first establish the digit-sum fact that gives the required minimality for \(n=2,3,4\).

### 1. A digit-sum lemma modulo divisors of \(81\)

For a finite digit list
\[
L=(d_0,d_1,\ldots,d_{\ell-1}),
\]
write
\[
S(L)=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}d_i,
\qquad
W(L)=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1} i d_i.
\]
The second quantity is a weighted digit sum. If \(L^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is the reversed list, then
\[
W(L^{\mathrm{rev}})=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}(\ell-1-i)d_i.
\]
Consequently,
\[
W(L)+W(L^{\mathrm{rev}})+S(L)=\ell S(L). \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the coefficient of every \(d_i\) on the left is
\(i+(\ell-1-i)+1=\ell\).

Let \(N\) be any positive divisor of \(81\). Since \(10=1+9\), for every \(i\ge0\) the binomial expansion gives
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod N. \tag{2}
\]
All terms of binomial degree at least two contain \(9^2=81\), and therefore vanish modulo \(N\). It follows that the integer represented by \(L\) satisfies
\[
\sum_i d_i10^i\equiv S(L)+9W(L)\pmod N. \tag{3}
\]
The reversed list has the same ordinary digit sum, so likewise
\[
\sum_i d_{\ell-1-i}10^i
   \equiv S(L)+9W(L^{\mathrm{rev}})\pmod N. \tag{4}
\]

Now take \(N=3^j\) and assume \(3^j\mid81\). Suppose \(m>0\), \(3^j\mid m\), and \(3^j\mid R(m)\). Let \(L\) be the decimal digit list of \(m\), in increasing place-value order, let \(\ell\) be its length, and abbreviate \(S=S(L)\), \(W=W(L)\), and \(W'=W(L^{\mathrm{rev}})\). Because \(m>0\), \(L\) is nonempty and \(\ell\ge1\). Equations (3) and (4), together with the two divisibility assumptions, yield
\[
S+9W\equiv0\pmod{3^j},
\qquad
S+9W'\equiv0\pmod{3^j}. \tag{5}
\]
Adding these and using (1), namely \(W+W'=(\ell-1)S\), gives
\[
0\equiv 2S+9(W+W')
 =2S+9(\ell-1)S
 =(9\ell-7)S\pmod{3^j}. \tag{6}
\]
But
\[
9\ell-7\equiv -7\equiv2\pmod3,
\]
so \(3\nmid 9\ell-7\). Hence \(9\ell-7\) is relatively prime to every power \(3^j\). We may therefore cancel this factor in (6), obtaining
\[
3^j\mid S(L). \tag{7}
\]
Thus, whenever \(3^j\mid81\), every positive integer divisible by \(3^j\) whose reversal is also divisible by \(3^j\) has digit sum divisible by \(3^j\).

### 2. A lower bound for valid multiples

Assume now that \(j\ge2\) and \(3^j\mid81\). Set
\[
s=3^{j-2},
\qquad
V_j=10^s-1.
\]
We claim that every positive \(m\) for which
\[
3^j\mid m
\quad\text{and}\quad
3^j\mid R(m)
\]
must satisfy
\[
m\ge V_j. \tag{8}
\]

Suppose to the contrary that \(m<V_j=10^s-1\). In particular \(m<10^s\), so the decimal expansion of \(m\) has at most \(s\) digits. Let its digit list have length \(\ell\le s\) and digit sum \(S\). Every digit is at most \(9\), hence
\[
S\le9\ell\le9s.
\]
Since \(s=3^{j-2}\),
\[
9s=3^2\cdot3^{j-2}=3^j. \tag{9}
\]
By (7), \(3^j\mid S\). Moreover \(S>0\), because \(m>0\) has at least one nonzero decimal digit. Therefore the positive multiple \(S\) of \(3^j\) satisfies \(S\le3^j\), and consequently
\[
S=3^j=9s. \tag{10}
\]

Since \(S\le9\ell\le9s\), equality in (10) forces \(\ell=s\). It also forces every one of the \(s\) digits to equal \(9\): if each digit is at most \(9\) and their sum is \(9s\), no digit can be smaller than \(9\). Thus \(m\) consists of exactly \(s\) copies of the digit \(9\), and therefore
\[
m=10^s-1=V_j,
\]
contrary to \(m<V_j\). This proves the lower bound (8).

### 3. The all-nines number is valid

We next show that
\[
3^{k+2}\mid 10^{3^k}-1 \qquad(k\ge0). \tag{11}
\]
This follows by induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\), the assertion is \(9\mid9\). Suppose it holds for \(k\), and put \(x=10^{3^k}\). Then
\[
10^{3^{k+1}}-1=x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1).
\]
By the induction hypothesis, \(3^{k+2}\mid x-1\). Also \(x\equiv1\pmod3\), because \(10\equiv1\pmod3\), so
\[
x^2+x+1\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Thus the product is divisible by \(3^{k+3}\), proving (11).

Apply (11) with \(k=j-2\). Since \(j\ge2\), this gives
\[
3^j\mid 10^{3^{j-2}}-1=V_j. \tag{12}
\]
The number \(V_j\) consists of \(s=3^{j-2}\) copies of the digit \(9\), so it is unchanged by reversal:
\[
R(V_j)=V_j. \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(V_j\) is a valid positive multiple of \(3^j\). Hence \(a(3^j)\le V_j\). Combined with the lower bound (8), which applies to every valid positive multiple, this gives
\[
a(3^j)=V_j=10^{3^{j-2}}-1 \tag{14}
\]
whenever \(j\ge2\) and \(3^j\mid81\).

In particular, \(3^2=9\), \(3^3=27\), and \(3^4=81\) all divide \(81\). Therefore (14) proves the desired equality for
\[
j=2,\quad j=3,\quad j=4.
\]
Explicitly, these values are the one-digit, three-digit, and nine-digit all-nines numbers, respectively.

### 4. A repeated palindromic block for every \(n\ge5\)

It remains to show that the proposed all-nines number is not minimal once \(n\ge5\). We construct a smaller valid multiple.

Consider the 27-digit palindrome
\[
B=100000001979999979100000001.
\]
Its digit list, written from units upward, is
\[
(1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,1,9,7,9,9,9,9,9,7,9,1,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,1).
\]
This list has length \(27\), is equal to its reverse, begins and ends with \(1\), and contains zero digits. A direct division gives
\[
B=243\cdot411522641893004029218107,
\]
so
\[
3^5\mid B. \tag{15}
\]

For \(n\ge5\), put
\[
t=3^{n-5}.
\]
Form \(W_n\) by concatenating exactly \(t\) copies of this 27-digit block. Since each block is palindromic and all blocks are identical, reversing the entire concatenation reverses both the order of the blocks and the digits within each block, but neither operation changes the result. Hence
\[
R(W_n)=W_n. \tag{16}
\]
There is no loss of a leading digit because the most significant digit of every block, and in particular of the final block, is \(1\).

Algebraically, concatenation gives
\[
W_n=B\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}(10^{27})^i. \tag{17}
\]
We need the following elementary geometric-sum divisibility fact: if \(r\equiv1\pmod3\), then for every \(q\ge0\),
\[
3^q\mid \sum_{i=0}^{3^q-1}r^i. \tag{18}
\]
To prove it, use induction on \(q\). For \(q=0\), the sum has one term and equals \(1\). If
\[
A_q=\sum_{i=0}^{3^q-1}r^i,
\]
then, grouping the \(3^{q+1}\) terms into three consecutive blocks of length \(3^q\),
\[
A_{q+1}=A_q\bigl(1+r^{3^q}+r^{2\cdot3^q}\bigr).
\]
Because \(r\equiv1\pmod3\), the second factor is congruent to \(1+1+1=0\pmod3\). Thus each induction step supplies one additional factor of \(3\), proving (18).

Take \(r=10^{27}\). Certainly \(r\equiv1\pmod3\). Applying (18) with \(q=n-5\), and recalling that \(t=3^{n-5}\), gives
\[
3^{n-5}\mid \sum_{i=0}^{t-1}(10^{27})^i. \tag{19}
\]
Combining (15), (17), and (19), we obtain
\[
3^n=3^5\cdot3^{n-5}\mid W_n. \tag{20}
\]
Together with (16), this shows that \(W_n\) is a valid positive multiple for the definition of \(a(3^n)\). Therefore
\[
a(3^n)\le W_n. \tag{21}
\]

We now compare \(W_n\) with the proposed all-nines number. Its number of digits is
\[
27t=27\cdot3^{n-5}=3^3\cdot3^{n-5}=3^{n-2}. \tag{22}
\]
Set \(s=3^{n-2}\). Any number represented by \(s\) decimal digits is less than \(10^s\), so
\[
W_n\le10^s-1.
\]
Equality would mean that every one of its \(s\) digits is \(9\). But every copy of the block \(B\) contains zero digits. Since \(t>0\), the concatenation \(W_n\) contains a zero digit, and hence cannot equal the all-nines number. Consequently
\[
W_n<10^s-1=10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{23}
\]
From (21) and (23),
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\qquad(n\ge5). \tag{24}
\]
Thus the claimed equality fails for every \(n\ge5\).

### 5. Completion of the equivalence

Let \(n\ge2\). If \(n=2,3\), or \(4\), equation (14) gives
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Conversely, suppose this equality holds. If \(n\) were not \(2,3\), or \(4\), then the assumption \(n\ge2\) would force \(n\ge5\). But (24) would then give the strict inequality
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore \(n\in\{2,3,4\}\), completing the proof.
